title: An ultrafine-grained ferrite network heterostructure enables ultrahigh strength and ductility in a medium-Mn lightweight steel
abstract: Simultaneous enhancement of strength and ductility in steels remains a critical challenge in materials science. In this study, a network heterostructure consisting of ultrafine-grained ferrite (∼300 nm) surrounding martensite and retained austenite was successfully constructed in a Fe-0.40C-5.91Mn-3.02Al-1.05Si-0.095Mo-0.048Nb-0.056Ti (wt.%) steel via deformation-induced ferrite transformation (DIFT) during warm rolling. After tempering at 200°C, the steel exhibited an exceptional strength-ductility synergy. The tempered steel displayed continuous yielding during tension, achieving an ultimate tensile strength of 2216 MPa and a total elongation of 21.0%, with a density reduction of approximately 5% relative to conventional steels. The exceptional work hardening capacity and ductility primarily stem from two factors. First, the soft network ferrite preferentially accommodates plastic strain, effectively shielding the retained austenite within network pockets and delaying the TRIP effect until higher strain levels, thereby providing sustained work hardening. Second, the network heterostructure induces substantial hetero-deformation-induced (HDI) strengthening, which delivers the high and persistent work hardening rate. This work demonstrates that the network heterostructure constitutes an effective pathway for enhancing the strength-ductility synergy in medium-Mn lightweight steels, providing a new strategy for the design of next-generation automotive steels.
